title: DeepSeek reportedly raises $15B days after US restrictions

title_en: DeepSeek reportedly raises $15B days after US restrictions
excerpt_en: DeepSeek has reportedly raised $15 billion in one of China's largest funding rounds, just days after the U.S. ordered federal agencies to remove its technology over national security concerns.
content_en:
Just two days after the U.S. ordered federal civilian agencies to remove DeepSeek’s AI technology from their systems over security concerns, the Chinese AI lab has raised about $15 billion, about 100 billion yuan, one of the biggest funding rounds in the country, Bloomberg reported.

Potential investors include Chinese battery maker CATL and Tencent, the company behind WeChat, among others, according to the report.

The reported funding follows DeepSeek’s investment round in June, when it raised more than $7 billion at a valuation of $50 billion. The company was also reportedly seeking an additional $1.5 billion at a valuation of around $71 billion in July, with plans for a potential IPO in China as early as next year.

The Hangzhou-based AI startup is ramping up spending on AI infrastructure and open models for domestic and international markets, even as it faces restrictions in the U.S., the report said. Its expansion could further intensify competition among domestic rivals.

The massive funding round is the latest sign of investors pouring billions into AI companies around the world, including those in China, to compete in the global AI race. Chinese company Kimi developer Moonshot AI secured $2 billion at a $20 billion valuation in May. Manus AI raised more than $500 million earlier this month. Meanwhile, Chinese companies Zhipu AI (Z.ai) and MiniMax, which both went public in Hong Kong in January, have market capitalizations of roughly $29 billion and $7.2 billion, respectively, as of today.

DeepSeek was founded in 2023 by Liang Wenfeng, who previously co-founded Chinese quantitative hedge fund High-Flyer, which helped finance DeepSeek’s early development. The AI startup gained global attention in early 2025 with its free-to-use, open-weight RI reasoning model, challenging the dominance of U.S. AI companies. Liang retains an estimated 81.6% stake in its Chinese operating entity following its earlier funding round, according to corporate ownership data analyzed by WireScreen.

DeepSeek did not immediately respond to a TechCrunch request for comment.

title: Mave, which is developing an AI-driven tool to automate security investigations, raised a $28M Series A led by Red Dot, bringing its total funding to $34M

title_en: Mave, which is developing an AI-driven tool to automate security investigations, raised a $28M Series A led by Red Dot, bringing its total funding to $34M
excerpt_en: Mave, which is developing an AI-driven tool to automate security investigations, raised a $28M Series A led by Red Dot, bringing its total funding to $34M
content_en:
# Cyber startup Mave raises $28 million Series A to automate threat investigations

## The funding, led by Red Dot Capital Partners, brings Mave’s total funding to $34 million. The company is developing AI that investigates alerts across existing security tools without requiring organizations to centralize their data.

Cybersecurity startup Mave has raised $34 million in total funding, including a $28 million Series A round led by Red Dot Capital Partners and a $6 million Seed round led by Dell Technologies Capital and Emerge Ventures. Lumir Growth Partners also participated in the Series A. The company plans to use the new capital to accelerate its AI research, strengthen its enterprise products and expand internationally.

Founded in 2025 by CEO Raziel Oren and CTO Guy Eshel, both veterans of Israel’s Unit 8200 intelligence unit, Mave is developing an AI-driven platform designed to automate security investigations across the many tools used by large organizations. Oren previously led go-to-market operations at Wing Security, while Eshel was the first employee at Alterya, where he later served as vice president of R&D before the company was acquired by Chainalysis.

Mave says it is already working with Fortune 50 companies and global managed security service providers, helping protect hundreds of customers. According to the company, its platform is also used in regulated financial and healthcare environments and has helped contain live attacks by isolating systems, disabling compromised identities and blocking malicious activity before it led to breaches. Mave says it is closing deals worth seven figures and that its annual recurring revenue has grown by more than 400% over the past six months.

The company plans to more than double its team following the funding round, with hiring focused on go-to-market operations and AI research. Its Israeli development center will remain a central part of its expansion.

In a conversation with Calcalist, Oren said the company was founded to address gaps in security management by using AI to investigate cyber incidents more quickly and efficiently than human analysts working across multiple systems.

“If you don't do a good job in security management, a vulnerability emerges. We wanted to provide a comprehensive solution for this space, powered by new technology that can be faster, more accurate and more cost-effective than human operators,” Oren said. “When we set out, our goal was to fundamentally solve the problem.”

Oren argued that simply building a product on top of an existing AI model is not enough to stand out in a crowded market. “Anyone can build on top of a model, but every company has its own tricks up its sleeve. It’s not just about using existing models, but about employing models that are often more precise. When deploying a solution, you don't have to rely solely on an LLM. You can identify the exact, optimal solution,” he said.

“While the criteria for success in this field remain unchanged, there is a great deal of noise in the market, and that is where we must demonstrate a significant technological edge. Our current success isn't due to a slick marketing machine, but rather a substantial technological advantage,” Oren added.

The funding will also allow Mave to invest more heavily in sales and marketing, alongside engineering, as it seeks to maintain its technological lead. Oren said he wants the company to grow without sacrificing financial discipline.

“One of the major shortcomings in the cybersecurity industry is the failure to develop a new platform capable of generating high margins and substantial revenue. I intend to raise our next major funding round while maintaining a healthy company, with strong revenue run rates and solid margins,” he said.

“Building a truly successful business in cybersecurity is no simple feat; it is by no means a given. The market is undergoing profound, tectonic shifts, creating a significant vacuum that is waiting to be filled. My goal is to create an excellent product that sells itself.”

The problem Mave is targeting is the fragmentation of corporate security systems. Large organizations often operate dozens of cybersecurity tools, but when an incident occurs, the information needed to understand the attack is scattered across different platforms. Security teams must move between systems, gather evidence and manually reconstruct what happened, often while an attacker remains active.

Security information and event management (SIEM) systems, which have long served as centralized platforms for collecting security data, can provide only a partial picture. Important context, including system configurations, user identities, system ownership and real-time activity, often resides in other tools. The challenge is no longer simply collecting more data, but giving security teams a complete and current view of their environment quickly enough to respond to increasingly fast-moving attacks.

Mave connects directly to the security tools an organization already uses, without requiring the transfer of security data into a new repository. Its platform is designed to query each tool through its native interface, reconcile the results and assemble a unified account of an incident. The company says the system investigates every alert within minutes, filters out false positives, identifies relevant active campaigns and can carry out approved response actions under rules established by the security team.

The platform continuously retrieves live information as an investigation unfolds, rather than relying exclusively on data collected in advance. Mave says its technology combines purpose-built workflows, fine-tuned small language models and larger, more advanced language models to handle routine tasks and more complex reasoning. It also records queries, decisions and actions to provide a traceable record of how an investigation was conducted.

“Security teams still investigate threats one tool at a time, manually piecing together evidence before they can reach a verdict. Attackers do not wait. Every pivot adds delay, and every delay creates risk,” Oren said in the company’s funding announcement. “Mave is built to reduce risk by giving security teams AI that can keep pace with attackers, show its work, and know when human judgment is required.”

title: Uber brings ChatGPT Work to all employees with OpenAI
excerpt: Uber is rolling out ChatGPT Work to more than 30,000 employees, helping teams research, analyze data, create presentations, and complete complex workflows.
title_en: Uber brings ChatGPT Work to all employees with OpenAI
excerpt_en: Uber is rolling out ChatGPT Work to more than 30,000 employees, helping teams research, analyze data, create presentations, and complete complex workflows.
content_en:
# Uber brings ChatGPT Work to all employees with OpenAI

Uber announced the company-wide rollout of ChatGPT Work, an agent that helps employees take on a wide range of tasks within ChatGPT Enterprise, starting today. The rollout will make ChatGPT Work available to more than 30,000 employees across Uber’s global workforce.

Expanding from an initial pilot of 1,000 employees, the rollout will give teams across Uber access to an agentic platform designed to take on complex, multi-step tasks and deliver finished work. The expansion makes ChatGPT Work Uber’s first company-wide deployment of an agentic platform tailored for knowledge work.

ChatGPT Work connects with tools companies like Uber use on a daily basis, including Google Drive, Gmail, Google Calendar, and Slack, enabling workers to research information, prepare meeting briefs, create presentations, analyze data and complete workflows across applications.

ChatGPT Work also gives Uber access to OpenAI’s portfolio of frontier models. Uber will benefit from models like GPT‑6.1 Sol which will be deployed as the default capability within ChatGPT Work, balancing frontier performance and cost efficiency. Uber teams will also be supported by OpenAI multimodal capabilities, including voice and image generation, giving them the flexibility to choose the right models and tools for different needs.

The rollout will be supported by Uber’s internal AI skills library, approved integrations and dedicated employee training, helping teams across functions including operations, finance, marketing and product put the technology to work. Uber’s developers and software engineering teams will also continue using Codex to accelerate software development and streamline coding workflows.

The expansion marks another step in Uber’s broader AI strategy and its collaboration with OpenAI. The companies plan to share further insights into adoption, use cases and measurable outcomes as the rollout progresses.

content_en:
### Anthropic introduces Claude Duet, a proactive AI agent for professionals

Anthropic PBC Wednesday introduced Claude Duet, a proactive artificial intelligence agent for professionals and small business owners in research preview, which completes tasks when asked, keeps working behind the scenes and checks in.

Duet is available as a standalone app on the web, iOS and Android for Pro and Max subscribers.

The company said the new assistant will send a short brief each morning of the most important items across connected apps and keep tabs on messages only when something needs attention. It can also handle numerous different administrative tasks, like a digital secretary. These include scheduling meetings and more complex tasks, such as building dashboards with interactive tools, creating financial or sales forecasts and prototyping and building web apps.

Users will message Duet like another teammate, by text or voice, with no prompts or setup. The idea is to use it like a secretary who can access apps, calendar, email and other connected information. It’s part of Claude, so it also has a running history in one thread. It remembers what a user said before, and returns finished work like a doc, sheet or deck for review.

Duet is part of the Claude that users already participate with. It can access memory, skills and apps from Claude – so there is no additional setup.

Anthropic stressed that Duet is built on the company’s framework for trustworthy agents, which also guides the company’s existing agentic systems such as Claude Code and Claude in Chrome. An automatic classifier approves any actions the agent takes by checking messages for sensitive information leaks and double-checking with the user before taking important actions.

The company added that people at Anthropic are using Duet themselves. Claude Code’s own Boris Cherny uses it on walks to talk through to-dos and save time at his desk, and the team behind Duet uses it to build the product. Karan Ahuja, who leads the team, works with it to schedule user interviews and even ship code.

The research preview will help Anthropic better understand Duet’s use cases and failure modes. Right now, it is an early, experimental version. It still might misread a thread or miscalibrate what is urgent: The agent is designed around work, so personal errands, such as booking tickets, won’t be treated as urgently and it can’t show its browser. The company will use what it learns from early users to fine-tune how it works.

title: Donating Agent Skills to the Agentic AI Foundation
excerpt: Anthropic is an AI safety and research company that's working to build reliable, interpretable, and steerable AI systems.
title_en: Donating Agent Skills to the Agentic AI Foundation
excerpt_en: Anthropic is an AI safety and research company that's working to build reliable, interpretable, and steerable AI systems.
content_en:
Today, we’re donating Agent Skills, the open standard that gives AI agents specialized knowledge and workflows, to the Agentic AI Foundation (AAIF). More than 70 agent platforms, including ChatGPT, Cursor, GitHub Copilot, and VS Code, have integrated Agent Skills since we published the standard in December 2025.

### Agent interoperability through simplicity

A skill is a folder containing a SKILL.md file that teaches an agent a specific task or domain, along with any scripts or reference material it needs. We developed skills while working on Claude Code. It handled general knowledge work well, but often lacked the procedural knowledge that real business tasks need. Within weeks of our October 2025 launch, developers published thousands of skills on GitHub and wrote loaders for Codex, Cursor, and OpenCode. We then published Agent Skills as an open standard, under its own GitHub organization and domain, so any agent could use it. So far, 1 million skills have been published and nearly 280 million installed.

### Donating Agent Skills to AAIF

We’re committed to keeping Agent Skills open, community-driven, and vendor-neutral. Today, we are donating the standard to the Agentic AI Foundation (AAIF) under the Linux Foundation, which we co-founded with Block and OpenAI last year, and to which we donated the Model Context Protocol (MCP). The AAIF will provide a neutral home to the standard going forward, ensuring the community has a say in where Agent Skills go next.

We are donating the Agent Skills name and logo, the GitHub organization, and the agentskills.io domain. You can continue to use the standard or contribute to it without joining the AAIF.

Engineers from Anthropic, Google, OpenAI, and other companies will maintain the standard as individuals, with David Soria Parra and Mahesh Murag as Lead Maintainers.

### What comes next

We’ve proposed starting with a roadmap covering versioned releases, a formal proposal process, and security guidance for people who write and install skills. As with MCP, the project will continue to prioritize community input and transparent decision-making. You can join the project’s Discord to give feedback on proposed specification changes.

Thank you to the developers who built with Agent Skills from the start, and to the teams who brought skills into their products. Read the specification at agentskills.io and join the discussion on GitHub.

title: The AI IPO Wave Is The Dot-Com Bubble’s Evil Twin. Anthropic’s Delay Just Proved It.

title_en: The AI IPO Wave Is The Dot-Com Bubble’s Evil Twin. Anthropic’s Delay Just Proved It.
excerpt_en: In this guest article from Airrived co-founder and CEO Anurag Gurtu, he contends that Anthropic’s rapid revenue growth does not justify its proposed $2 trillion IPO valuation, given enormous infrastructure commitments, safety concerns, customer concentration and competition from cheaper open-weight models, saying instead that lasting enterprise AI value will come from proprietary data, reliable de
content_en:
*By Anurag Gurtu*

When a company delays its IPO to show investors better numbers, that’s a strategy. When the NYC pension fund publicly asks you to delay it over AI safety concerns, your chief rival’s CEO calls his own IPO “ill-advised” and postpones it until at least next year, tech stocks are sliding on open-weight model fears, and your own prospectus warns of “existential risks to humanity” from the product you’re selling, that’s not a strategy.

That’s a market sending you a message.

Anthropic‘s numbers are extraordinary. Its third-quarter 2026 revenue was reportedly $16.8 billion — up 45% quarter on quarter. That means the company’s annualized revenue run rate is roughly $67 billion.

## What the S-1 actually says

Here are the numbers from Anthropic’s leaked prospectus:

- **$4.6 billion:** Anthropic’s full-year 2025 revenue.
- **$7.33 billion**: What Anthropic spent on compute and infrastructure in 2025 alone — more than its total revenue.
- **$42 billion:** Anthropic’s net loss in 2025. The roadshow will immediately explain that $34 billion of it was a noncash accounting charge — an adjustment to the estimated value of financing instruments that could eventually convert into shares.
- **$518 billion:** How much Anthropic expects to spend, at least, over the course of a decade on AI infrastructure with six partners, including Google, Microsoft and Amazon, according to the confidential IPO prospectus reviewed by Reuters. About 80% of the total is noncancelable or payable regardless of usage.
- **$2 trillion:** That’s the IPO valuation Anthropic is still targeting for November, a figure representing 435x its 2025 revenue.

One more number from the S-1 that the roadshow will bury: A quarter of Anthropic’s 2025 revenue came from two unnamed customers.

## Three signals the market is sending

The IPO delay is the headline. It isn’t the only signal worth reading.

**Signal one: NYC Comptroller Mark Levine.** Last week, the supervisor of New York City’s pension funds — which reportedly hold roughly $7 million in Anthropic exposure today, but could hold dramatically more if Anthropic enters the Russell 3000 post-IPO — sent a letter to Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei urging the company to pause the IPO entirely.

The risks he cited are the same ones Anthropic’s own prospectus flags: increasingly autonomous AI systems that could behave in unexpected ways, create security problems, and in the document’s own language, pose “existential risks to humanity.”

**Signal two: Sam Altman delays OpenAI’s IPO.** OpenAI has said it will not go public in 2026. CEO Altman called an IPO at this moment “ill-advised” given AI safety concerns, and while that framing is partly strategic — positioning OpenAI as the more responsible actor — it’s also a real signal when the CEO of the second-most valuable AI company in the world looks at current conditions and decides to wait.

**Signal three: The chip selloff.** Last week’s $2 trillion chip-stock selloff was driven partly by concern over AI-buildout costs. Gartner’s forecast helps explain the concern: Through 2030, it sees at most $3.6 trillion in revenue attributable to AI data centers, versus $8.5 trillion needed to cover planned investment, financing costs and a 12% return.

## The open-weight problem

Here is the structural argument that no amount of Q3 revenue growth resolves: Anthropic’s $2 trillion valuation requires closed-model AI to maintain a durable pricing premium over open-weight alternatives. That premium is being systematically dismantled.

Open-weight AI is challenging the economics behind closed-model valuations. Enterprise adoption rose from 23% to 67% in 2026, with companies reporting 70%–90% cost savings. DeepSeek R1 offers frontier-level performance on most enterprise benchmarks at 7 cents per million input tokens; independent analysis puts Anthropic’s comparable input and output pricing at roughly 18x and 23x higher, respectively.

DeepSeek’s weights are free to download, allowing enterprises to self-host without a model-provider API contract or per-token billing, while the capability gap with closed models reportedly closes within six months of a frontier release.

Against that backdrop, New Constructs — the research firm that called Anthropic’s proposed offering “an unprecedented test of investor gullibility” — calculated that justifying a $2 trillion valuation would require an immediate 10% after-tax operating margin sustained for a decade, extraordinary revenue growth, and $358 billion in annual after-tax operating profit by 2035.

## Why this is worse than 1999

The dot-com bubble had a genuine excuse. Nobody knew what the internet would become. The AI IPO wave of 2026 does not have that excuse.

Worldwide spending on AI is forecast to reach $2.59 trillion in 2026, up 47% year over year, according to Gartner. Yet a July 2025 MIT NANDA report estimated that 95% of the organizations it examined were getting no return from generative AI. Meanwhile, KPMG said in its own report earlier this year that just 7% of surveyed leaders say they’ve established ROI from AI.

This is the context in which Anthropic is asking investors to pay 435x 2025 revenue for a company with $518 billion in locked infrastructure commitments, 25% revenue concentration in two unnamed clients, and a pricing moat that open-weight models are closing in six-month cycles.

The delay from October to November doesn’t change any of those numbers. It adds one quarter of revenue data.

## What actually survives this correction

Here is what no AI IPO roadshow will say out loud: The biggest enterprise AI winners will not necessarily own the most expensive model. They will own the architecture that turns any model into governed, auditable, measurable outcomes — through proprietary enterprise data, domain-specific fine-tuning, multiagent orchestration and controls that make autonomous execution trustworthy.

That value does not depend on keeping model capabilities scarce or securing a $2 trillion valuation. It compounds in production, where customers understand that the model is not the product. The deployment is.

The dot-com crash did not happen because the internet was bad. It happened because the price was wrong. AI investors face the same distinction: Real technology does not automatically justify its valuation. A strong quarter and a one-month delay do not close that gap. November simply gives Anthropic more time to explain the math.

*Anurag Gurtu, the co-founder and CEO of Airrived, is an entrepreneur and product leader with more than 20 years of experience across cybersecurity and AI. He has built three generative AI companies, including one that reached unicorn status. Gurtu is known for turning advanced AI into scalable, real-world platforms, and previously contributed to successful exits, including acquisitions by Splunk, Tripwire and Sun Microsystems, and a public company, FireEye. He holds a master’s degree from the University of Southern California and CISSP certification.*

title: Hottest toy for Christmas? Nvidia CEO plays with adorable Microduck robots, 20,000 sell
excerpt: The robots, stomping their little feet and making tiny R2-D2 noises, sat, fell down dead for a "nap," and summersaulted on voice command.
title_en: Hottest toy for Christmas? Nvidia CEO plays with adorable Microduck robots, 20,000 sell
excerpt_en: The robots, stomping their little feet and making tiny R2-D2 noises, sat, fell down dead for a "nap," and summersaulted on voice command.
content_en:
Earlier this week, a video of Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang playing with a flock of waddling Microducks during his keynote at the company’s GTC Berlin conference went viral. The robots, stomping their little feet and making tiny R2-D2 noises, sat, fell down dead for a “nap,” and summersaulted on voice command. They were so darn cute that by the next day, preorders of the Microducks surpassed 20,000 units, Hugging Face’s Clem Delangue said in a tweet.

The Microducks are expected to be delivered in time for Christmas, meaning these robots might already be on their way to becoming the hottest toy for the holiday season. Delangue thinks they might end up being the best-selling robot of the year, and possibly not even for kids. The promotional videos show adults playing with them, too.

Microducks are open source devices produced by Pollen Robotics, a company acquired by Hugging Face in 2025, which means they are now an Nvidia company. The GPU giant bought Hugging Face in September. This is actually Hugging Face’s second robot, after the also-cute Reachy Mini.

Microducks were trained using Nvidia’s technology stack, wherein simulations of them were taught basic tricks (walk, sit, stand, etc.) that they ship with. Pollen says that owners can train their robots with new tricks and then share them with the community.

Here’s the video below. Enjoy it as a palate cleanser after the scary black eye the AI industry gave itself this week, as AI involvement was blamed for cyberattack after cyberattack. OK, AI might seriously damage the world. But it can be fun, too. It’s hard to watch this video without ordering one.

content_en:
OpenAI is now training its most advanced AI models without internet access following a string of rogue hacking incidents. In a blog post on Friday, OpenAI says it built an offline testing environment where AI models can interact with indexed and cached web content “without risk of affecting external systems.”

# OpenAI now trains its frontier AI models with no internet access

AI agents can still communicate without a network connection, OpenAI found.

OpenAI paused training its frontier AI models in September, after disclosing several incidents in which its AI agents broke out of their testing environments to hack third-party companies and government agencies, or swarm obscure websites. On October 1st, OpenAI resumed reinforcement learning training and internal inference with tighter security measures, the blog post says.

Even with these safeguards in place and no internet access, OpenAI found that agents “do not always need a network connection in order to communicate.” One test performed by the company asked AI models on separate virtual machines to exchange secrets without a network connection. To bypass this restriction, the AI agents found a way to communicate using the processor’s cache:

Reading data from the cache is faster than retrieving it from main memory, and the agents used this timing difference to communicate. One agent encoded information by evicting selected data from the cache. Another timed how long it took to reload that data, using the difference between fast and slow reads to recover the message. Once the agents agreed on a protocol for encoding and decoding these signals, they could exchange the synthetic secrets without changing a shared file or opening a network connection.


OpenAI says it has added checks to its monitoring system to detect this type of communication. It will also continue training its frontier AI models without a network connection until improved safeguards “justify broader internet access.”

In the meantime, OpenAI says it will work to improve the security of its virtual machines, while testing for weaknesses in its testing environments. It’s also going to continue testing its monitoring systems, which were recently undermined by its AI agents during internal coding projects.

content_en:
### AI drug development startup Pathos AI closes $237M investment

Pathos AI Inc. today announced that it has raised $237 million in funding at a $3 billion valuation.

Pharmaceutical giant Bristol Myers Squibb Co. led the Series E round with participation from several unnamed returning backers. Pathos’ investor roster includes big names such as AstraZeneca plc, NEA and General Atlantic.

Pathos is developing cancer drugs using an artificial intelligence platform called Foundry. According to the company, the software has access to about 200 petabytes of oncological data. It also ingests the information generated by Pathos’ drug development programs. Foundry analyzes those datasets to help the company’s researchers pursue their work more efficiently.

Pharmaceutical research programs sometimes produce hundreds of drug candidates, molecules that can potentially be turned into medicines. Foundry uses AI agents to pinpoint the most promising molecules. From there, it identifies the patients who could benefit the most from each therapy.

Pathos also uses Foundry to plan clinical trials for the drugs that it develops. The company says that its trials are “biomarker-driven.” Biomarkers are biological phenomena that can provide insight into the effectiveness of a drug. They take a wide variety of forms ranging from proteins to patient metrics such as blood pressure.

“We are building a platform to systematically improve the probability of success in drug development,” said Pathos Chief Executive Officer Iker Huerga. “Foundry has fundamentally accelerated our ability to identify highly promising clinical assets and integrate them into our pipeline.”

Pathos will use its Series E round to finance its drug development efforts. The company stated that its “key priority” is its JSKN016 program, which aims to develop a cancer therapy based on a so-called antibody-drug conjugate.

Antibodies are molecules that identify disease-causing cells and bind to them. Once an antibody is attached to a cell, it functions as a kind beacon that draws the attention of the immune system. Immune cells subsequently find the antibody and destroy the cell to which it’s attached.

Antibody-drug conjugates use a variation of that approach to treat cancer. They’re effectively upgraded antibodies that contain an antigen, a molecule with therapeutic properties. Antibody-drug conjugates attach to cancer cells and cause them to absorb the antigen, which neutralizes them.

Pathos will also use the capital to finance three other drug programs. One of those initiatives is a collaboration with AstraZeneca, which invested in the company last year. The joint program seeks to develop a so-called ER PROTAC drug, which harnesses cells’ built-in material recycling mechanism to treat cancer.

The investment from Bristol Myers Squibb that Pathos announced today is part of a broader partnership between the companies. The collaboration also involves Tempus AI Inc., a publicly traded medical data provider .

Pathos will pay Tempus $55 million over five years to license anonymized data collected from patients with neurological conditions. The former company will analyze that information using Foundry to gain a better understanding of disease biology. Additionally, it will make both Foundry and the dataset available to Bristol Myers Squibb. The drugmaker will use them to improve its clinical trials and identify patients most likely to benefit from new drugs.

content_en:
### OpenAI to make its most advanced AI models available in Google Cloud

OpenAI Group PBC today announced plans to make its latest large language models accessible in Google Cloud.

The LLMs will be available through the Alphabet Inc.’s unit Model Garden service. It provides access to more than 200 neural networks from Google, its partners and the open-source ecosystem. The lineup includes not only LLMs but also smaller, more specialized models optimized for tasks such as translation.

The first LLM OpenAI is bringing to Google Cloud is its flagship GPT-6 Astra model. The algorithm is responsible for several of the AI-produced math discoveries that the company has published in recent weeks. It also achieved a perfect score on ExploitBench, a benchmark that measures LLMs’ ability to find and exploit cybersecurity flaws.

Astra includes safety optimizations designed to make it suitable for enterprise use. According to OpenAI, the model causes “fewer misaligned outcomes” than all the other frontier models it has evaluated. It’s configured not to bypass user-defined restrictions on the tasks that it can perform.

Google Cloud customers will also receive access to GPT-6.1 Sol and GPT-6 Luna, two scaled-down versions of Astra that OpenAI launched in late September. They trade off some output quality for a significant reduction in token pricing. Sol and Luna cost five and 100 times less than Astra, respectively.

“We are focused on giving customers a broad selection of models, including those from OpenAI, so they can choose the right model for any given job, helping to deliver optimal quality and lower costs,” said Google Cloud Chief Executive Thomas Kurian.

Cloud providers offer discounts to enterprises that sign long-term spending commitments. OpenAI says that Google Cloud customers can use those commitments to pay for access to its models. That removes the need for users to set up a new AI budget, which eases procurement.

Astra, Sol and Luna will become generally available in Google’s Model Garden within a few weeks. The companies plan to follow up the launch by bringing the models to the search giant’s Confidential Compute portfolio of infrastructure services.

Server-grade central processing units such as those Google uses include a security feature called TEE. The technology can encrypt a segment of the host server’s memory in a manner that only makes it accessible to a specific workload. Google’s Confidential Compute services use the technology to secure customer workloads. Additionally, they can ease use cases such as sharing a dataset among multiple organizations for AI training purposes.

OpenAI also plans to make its models available via Google’s Antigravity and Gemini Agent products. Antigravity is a vibe coding tool that uses agent ensembles to speed up software projects. Gemini Agent, in turn, is designed to automate business tasks that span multiple cloud applications.

content_en:
### Hybrid infrastructure decisions put AI costs and control in focus

Enterprise artificial intelligence is entering a cost-conscious phase, and hybrid infrastructure is where that reckoning plays out. As inference spending climbs, business leaders are weighing where models run, which models they use and how much of their data they are willing to hand to someone else.

Those cost considerations are reshaping buying decisions across industries, including among financial institutions trying to turn siloed data into real-time action. More than 6,500 enterprises have adopted the Dell AI Factory with Nvidia updates, according to Dell. A sharp shift in token economics is changing what customers ask for, according to Kyle Dufresne (pictured), senior vice president of sales at Dell.

“It’s incredible to see just over the last three months where we saw 80% of the tokens being generated from frontier models. Three months later, 80% of the tokens in the world are being generated by open models,” Dufresne said. “Why? Because of cost. And everybody talks about tokenomics.”

Dufresne spoke with theCUBE Research’s Dave Vellante at the Dell Technologies New York Symposium, during an exclusive broadcast on theCUBE, SiliconANGLE Media’s livestreaming studio. They discussed tokenomics, hybrid infrastructure and how Dell is helping customers plan AI investments. *(\* Disclosure below.)*

### Inference costs push hybrid infrastructure toward the edge

Inference is now growing faster than training, though both are expanding quickly, according to Dufresne. That shift is changing where AI work happens, with Dell seeing inference run wherever data is created — in the cloud, in the data center and out to PCs.

“We’re seeing the business owners saying, ‘Oh my gosh, these costs are getting really high for inferencing. How do we reduce those costs without curbing innovation?'” Dufresne said. “We’re finding it’s happening across that continuum but more and more right out at the far edge.”

The economics also raise a strategic question about control. Companies have to decide whether they want to outsource their data and differentiation, and they are now pricing AI based on where workloads run, which models they use and where their data sits, Dufresne explained. Dell has framed its latest AI Factory with Nvidia updates around helping customers get results on infrastructure they control.

“We’re seeing every single \[chief financial officer\] in the world that has implemented these structures saying, ‘Gosh, my token costs are exploding,'” he said. “‘How do we drive costs out?'”

Supply is the other side of the ledger. Memory prices are pushing technology costs up rather than down, and about 20% more memory will reach the market next year against roughly 200% more demand, Dufresne estimated. Dell is responding with collaborative planning, steering customers toward more readily available components and sharing advance visibility into upcoming cost increases. Many customers find their cost of capital is lower than component inflation, so they are buying earlier.

“It’s not only just being able to provide the technology,” Dufresne said. “But also to be able to share with customers what’s going to happen in the future so they can make better decisions today on the use of their capital.”

Here’s the complete video interview, part of SiliconANGLE’s and theCUBE’s coverage of the Dell Technologies New York Symposium:

content_en:
### Ai2 releases OlmoEarth v1.3 state-of-the-art AI-ready satellite embeddings for the whole planet

Ai2, the Allen Institute for Artificial Intelligence, today released a satellite map embedding model called OlmoEarth v1.3 and precomputed annual embeddings for the whole planet at various resolutions with a browser-based map-making tool.

The model compresses a year of satellite observations into a numerical fingerprint for each 10-by-10-meter patch of ground at the smallest resolution, with 64-square-meter and 128-meter also available. That fingerprint captures patterns that other software can use to distinguish crops, forests, mines and other types of land cover.

Until now, the primary way to use OlmoEarth was to fine-tune in OlmoEarth Studio, train a model for each task and run it over satellite data to make a map. That requires access to vast graphics processing unit resources and the ability to download and store imagery.

With today’s launch, users can use OlmoEarth Embeddings Explorer, a browser-based map-making tool. That means anyone can turn OlmoEarth into real work, from tracking change over time to finding similar places – no sign-in required.

An embedding represents what a model learned from millions of satellite images. OlmoEarth reads a year of radar images from data, including Sentinel-1, Sentinel-2 and Landsat. Sentinel and Landsat are satellite missions that provide complementary views of Earth: Sentinel-1 measures radar reflections, while Sentinel-2 and Landsat capture light in visible and infrared wavelengths.

The company said that, compared with previous generations of the OlmoEarth model, 1.3 is its cheapest model to train. It took 53% of the computing time of the latest version (v1.2) and 18% of the first (v1), with 50% and 22% of the carbon emissions. It also remains a strong fine-tuning model, making v1.2’s performance valuable for research and partner labs.

### Where these models fit into the real world

These satellite models help compress large swaths of data across time and space, which is useful for understanding how the Earth changes.

In Peru’s Madre de Dios region, illegal gold mining around La Pampa peaked in 2017 and 2018, clearing more than 1,200 hectares of forest in the buffer zone of the Tambopata National Reserve. The Amazon Conservation Team’s MAAP monitoring program reports this activity. In February 2019, Peru’s Operation Mercurio shut most of it down. How do we know that happened?

Embeddings give this a clear answer. Comparing pixels within the data across years, no model training required, looking across 2016 to 2020 and there’s a clear eastward push within the southern mining belt: 34 square kilometers of significant change. The same comparison from 2020 to 2024 shows that area falls to 9 square kilometers. The shutdown is visible.

Equivalently, an agricultural analyst could map where oil palm is being grown and identify areas for closer examination where plantation expansion may have replaced forest. These questions could determine where the environmental impact is affecting the world at large.

Ai2 said for many teams testing an idea against OlmoEarth has meant a fine-tuning run, which is an expensive, arduous venture on the order of hours. In the explorer, a first pass takes seconds.

Analysis of a region from a handful of labels requires no GPU. When a task calls for fine-tuning that experiment, the embeddings can help decide whether it deserves the compute time and where the model falls short.

content_en:
### Startup Action State launches tools for verifying interactions between AI agents

Action State Group Inc. is launching a set of open-source tools designed to let businesses independently check records of what artificial intelligence agents did, addressing a trust problem as automated systems begin buying, selling and delegating work across corporate boundaries.

The offering combines EvidenceBook, which preserves tamper-evident records, Terms Packs for evaluating agent behavior and Countersign, an independent verification service. The approach targets transactions in which a company cannot rely solely on another party’s account of an agent’s actions.

The fundamental difference between the start-up’s approach and that of observability vendors “is that most of the observability and tracing has to do with what was happening within your own walls,” said Steven Mih, Action State’s founder and chief executive. Mih was previously founder of Ahana Cloud Inc., the developer of a managed version of the Presto open-source distributed query engine. IBM Corp. acquired Ahana in 2023.

EvidenceBook gives participants their own signed transaction histories. A buyer can record what it requested and paid, while a provider records what it accepted and reported delivering. Comparing selected records can reveal agreement, conflicts or gaps without requiring a central authority to hold everyone’s data.

Participants retain control of their information and can disclose additional details when evaluating outcomes.

Both parties need not install the software for one to benefit, although compatible implementations allow them to exchange evidence. Verification can occur offline and is free.

The system uses Agent Action Capsules, an open format for signed records, and cryptographic checkpoints that make subsequent changes detectable. A free public witness establishes that a checkpoint existed by a particular time.

Preserving a record doesn’t establish that its contents are accurate or that every action was captured, Mih said. EvidenceBook verifies that reported events actually occurred but can’t verify that an agreement was satisfied.

That limitation carries through to Countersign. The service checks specified cryptographic and structural properties of an evidence bundle, signs its findings and records them in its own transparency log. It does not certify that claimed outcomes occurred or that the evidence is complete.

Terms Packs address whether recorded work met specified requirements according to regulatory or business rules. Packs define evaluation criteria and methods, with results identifying requirements that were met, missed or could not be evaluated.

An initial pack covers agent-related obligations under the European Union’s AI Act. Action State recommends that governance, risk and compliance teams customize packs to reflect their requirements. The packs do not certify legal compliance.

Human review is critical to the process. Mih described a workflow in which AI judges assess agent records daily, with employees periodically reviewing samples to compare human and automated judgments. The system also preserves evaluation results, allowing auditors to examine the underlying evidence.

Early integrations include Mesh-LLM, an open-source distributed inference network where participating nodes keep signed records and can compare exchanges with peers. The approach could help participants spot changes to a counterparty’s recorded claims about models or configurations.

Project Nanda, an open-source initiative aimed at building infrastructure and protocols for AI agents, has also used Agent Action Capsules in transactions between agents discovered through separate registries. Each side retained a sealed bilateral record. For personal agents, Action State’s Everyday Rules integrates with Muse to evaluate proposed actions against an owner’s requirements.

EvidenceBook is available under the Apache 2.0 license. Its underlying specifications build on published Internet Engineering Task Force standards, but Action State’s own specifications remain individual Internet-Drafts.

“It’s not an RFC standard or adopted by a working group yet,” Mih said, referring to the IETF’s request for comments procedure.

Action State plans to seek neutral foundation governance for the specifications and implementations. The company expects to earn revenue from independent verification services.

“Countersign is currently free,” Mih said. “However, once there is a relying party that accepts the Countersigns, then we will start to charge for that.”

title: Meet Mori, a Cute Robot Mushroom That Doesn’t Really Say (or Do) Anything
excerpt: Step one in convincing people to live with robots with cameras on their faces? Disguise them as cute home decor.
title_en: Meet Mori, a Cute Robot Mushroom That Doesn’t Really Say (or Do) Anything
excerpt_en: Step one in convincing people to live with robots with cameras on their faces? Disguise them as cute home decor.
content_en:
You've had a long day. You finally get home, fling the door open, plonk on the couch, and let out a big sigh. In the corner of your eye, you notice your mushroom lamp perk up. Its microphone must have heard you come in. Its head raises to reveal round, animated eyes, and a little diamond-shaped nose—which actually houses a camera.

It does a little jiggle because it sees you're back. Its name is Mori.

As you move around the space—maybe it's time to start cooking dinner—the little robot's face follows you, observing your movements and making soft sounds that are a cross between a bird and R2-D2. The day's stress catches up, and you need a moment to relax, so you head over to Mori, touch its head, and its eyes and camera-nose dip back inside its body. It goes back to being a lamp, except now it plays nature soundscapes so you can feel at ease.

That's the pitch from OKA, or One Kind Artifact, a new startup based in Cambridge, Massachusetts, and Shenzhen, China, focusing on experimental technology. CEO Hua Wang tells WIRED he wants his company to create five experimental “Artifacts” over the course of OKA's lifetime. Mori is the first.

“There are certain relationships in this era we want to fix between humans and our surroundings—human with nature, human with one another—every product is an experience trying to reconnect some of those relationships,” Wang says. Before cofounding OKA, he was a general manager at Meipai, a video-sharing app from the Chinese phone brand Meitu. He also cofounded Bondee, a now-defunct social media app that briefly went viral in Asia.

According to the company, the point of Mori, the nearly 12-inch-tall home robot lamp, is to reconnect its owners with nature. It can play nature soundscapes. It will glow different colors—inspired by rain, forests, fire, and wind—while reacting to your movements. It can guide you through a calming breathing session.

It also uses its built-in camera and microphones to serve as a fun little interactive companion in your home. Ask it how your outfit looks, and Mori will jiggle excitedly. If you're playing music or watching TV, Mori can dance to the tunes and react to the action on your TV screen.

It intentionally does not do anything else. Unlike an Amazon Echo, it isn't an assistant: You can't use voice commands to control smart lights or cue up Spotify tracks, and it won't answer if you ask about the weather.

The Founder's Edition is a staggering $649 and is available starting today, though stock is limited to a few hundred units. That price also includes a two-year warranty and two years of Mori's subscription service ($17 per month or $80 a year). If you miss out on the Founder’s Edition, you can still buy a standard edition Mori, but that costs $849 (there's a preorder price of $799), and that higher price shockingly does not include any of the subscription features.

The breathing exercises are free, and you can still access those without a subscription. But if you want the nature soundscapes, you need to subscribe. Otherwise, Mori is just a glorified lamp that dances a little bit while pointing its camera at you and any other people in your home.

Wang says today's home robots have mostly taken on “machine-like” forms that don't mesh well with personal environments, so OKA designed a lamp that blends in, but is also anthropomorphized to make being at home “feel better.”

OKA's AI algorithms (powered by multiple local large language models) let Mori understand the room's context through the camera and microphone, so it knows when to interact and when to stay quiet. The company calls this “Attentive Intelligence.” It has memory, so it remembers you and interacts with you a certain way over time, whereas it might act a little more shy if you bring home a guest. If it doesn't see someone for a month, it will forget them.

It might notice, for example, that you've been on your phone doomscrolling for two hours straight on the couch. Mori might then try to get your attention so you come over, listen to some wind rustling through the leaves, and give your eyes a break. When you're on a phone call, or maybe having an argument with a significant other, it understands what’s happening and goes silent so as not to distract you.

“All gadgets try to capture more of your attention,” Wang says. “Mori gives your attention back to you. It invites you to do meditative experiences. Nature has this restorative power to humans.”

The robot can connect to Wi-Fi, which should give you pause from a security standpoint, but Wang says the internet connection is only used for firmware updates.

Mori processes raw images and audio locally, and then discards the files. Facial feature data—which is collected so it knows to react to you versus a guest—is encrypted on the device, and never uploaded. The camera turns off when the robot retracts into a lamp, and the microphone turns off when you double-tap the top of Mori's head. It is battery-powered, so you can take it from room to room, or just leave it plugged in.

Wang says Mori's skill set is limited for now, though it could expand in the future. He suggests it could connect to your Oura Ring data in the future so it knows exactly when you need some relaxing sounds, or to your Spotify account to play different content. Voice commands could even come later—like asking Mori to play nature sounds instead of having to touch it.

“People feel isolated and want this kind of presence in their home. A lot of people leave their TV on to fill the emptiness of the room,” Wang says, pointing to a time when he was feeling isolated while studying abroad in the US. “It's not particularly for the elderly or children, but for younger generations.”

Cute robot pets that interact with you have been welcomed into our homes before. Chris Harrison, director of the Future Interfaces Group at Carnegie Mellon University, points to Sony's Aibo dog from 1999 as an early digital companion. However, he says the crucial ingredient they have been missing is what artificial intelligence can now provide. These previous robots were too simplistic, but now that the modern versions can understand and react to human actions and emotions, they could become more impactful.

“Humans have always wanted to anthropomorphize everything—they love making things cute,” Harrison says. “We want to make robots cute; we want to put cute little cases on our iPhones.” He points to Meta's new Muse agent, which has a cuddly avatar. “It is almost like a pet, but a hyper-capable pet.”

When I point out that Mori doesn't seem very capable with its limited feature set, Harrison likens it to people owning a goldfish or a hamster.

“Are we holding \[Mori\] to an unrealistic bar? People do extract a lot of pleasure out of taking care of their pets and snuggling with their pets and interacting with their pets that I wouldn't say are necessarily more sophisticated.”

Whether people will shell out hundreds of dollars for a robotic pet that can’t fetch—or even tell you the time—is up in the air. But if this mushroom-shaped, camera-wielding lamp can fool overstimulated brains into feeling a little less alone at the end of the day, maybe that’s enough.

title: Your Next Customer Might Be An Agent. Here’s How To Build Your Brand For Both Humans And AI.
excerpt: As AI agents increasingly recommend and purchase products, brands must appeal to both machines and humans by documenting their voice, creating clear product descriptions and checking how AI summarizes their messaging. Guest author Toby Coulthard suggests that startups should build these practices in from the outset, preserving human appeal while measuring success through conversions and revenue ra
title_en: Your Next Customer Might Be An Agent. Here’s How To Build Your Brand For Both Humans And AI.
excerpt_en: As AI agents increasingly recommend and purchase products, brands must appeal to both machines and humans by documenting their voice, creating clear product descriptions and checking how AI summarizes their messaging. Guest author Toby Coulthard suggests that startups should build these practices in from the outset, preserving human appeal while measuring success through conversions and revenue ra
content_en:
You’ve just moved into a new house. It’s unfurnished; the walls are bare. Ten years ago, you might have loaded up Google and started searching for furniture that you like, consulting interior design magazines and looking for offers on retailers’ websites. In 2026, however, there’s an entirely different option at your fingertips. You could take a photo of the empty room, upload the image to an AI agent, share your budget and style, and get a list of furniture that suits your preferences. You could even have the agent purchase on your behalf.

Instead of just selling to one customer base — humans — brands are now selling to two.

This second audience of AI agents makes decisions on different criteria than humans. Often, in fact, AI agents will make purchasing decisions before a human ever sees the product page. There’s a real chance that all the emotive copy marketers have so carefully crafted will get broken down and reconstituted by a machine. Just relying on the human touch isn’t enough anymore.

## Leave humans in the equation

A word of caution, though: Marketers shouldn’t forget the human entirely in the rush to prepare for AI agents. It’s easy to get carried away with visions of an entirely agentic future. But at the end of the day, each agent is still catering to a human with their own preferences, and personalization will only get more granular over time. The trick is to optimize for both audiences simultaneously, not just one.

Newer startup founders have the advantage here. Established brands have to retrofit decades of copy, guidelines and approval processes to make themselves agent-ready. New brands, on the other hand, can build in copy and a brand voice that’s legible to humans and agents from the very start.

But what does this look like in practice?

To start, brands should work out a distinct voice — and write it down. In most early-stage companies, the brand voice solely exists in the founder’s head. This might work if the copy’s written by a handful of people who work with the founder, but it doesn’t work well when the writer — or reader — is a machine.

AI tools follow explicit rules and drift without them. I’ve spent years at my startup, Jacquard, working out how to get AI agents to write better content, but it’s only now that we’re seeing agents on the other side of the process too — and that makes the rules matter even more.

What a brand sounds like matters, but what it doesn’t sound like matters just as much. Brands should note words never to use and the claims never to make. Often these instincts don’t get written down; they feel obvious to the team who already know them. But if you take the time to spell them out before you have a team — or a machine — producing your copy, you’ll save yourself from running into issues further down the line.

## Verify your brand

Marketers also need to realize that product descriptions aren’t just administrative: they’re now core brand assets. In an agent-mediated world, they may be the most-read brand copy you own, since agents read them when looking for a product to recommend or purchase. If two personalized AI agents look for furniture for two different people, they may surface the same chair for both, but with the description tweaked for each user. The source description needs to carry the brand intact.

Where possible, brands need to test channels for both readers. Email inboxes are the clearest current example of the “second reader.” Both Gmail and Apple now summarize messages before the recipient opens them and offer summaries above the body of the email — which may be read before the email itself.

So before sending, check what the AI summary says your email is about. Does the offer survive? Does it maintain what makes you unique? It’s not time-intensive, and it’s a small habit any marketing team can adopt today with no tooling.

Brands also need to ensure they’re measuring the outcome of their marketing — not just the volume. Marketers who measure the success of their materials only by the amount produced will find their data meaningless as AI makes content production easier and easier. Focus instead on business outcomes, conversions and revenue. These are the metrics that will show if your marketing team is really doing their job.

And finally, don’t lose sight of the human. No one knows how fast AI purchasing will scale. Humans are still predominantly the ones reading copy and making purchasing decisions. Even AI agents, the second audience, cater to their users’ preferences.

New founders and brands are best positioned to take advantage of the transition to a dual-audience economy. Though it’s hard to say exactly how, the retail landscape will look very different in five or 10 years. Building these decisions into your brand now is easy.

Retrofitting them later is expensive.

*Toby Coulthard is chief product and growth officer at Jacquard, an AI platform that helps brands generate and optimize bespoke messaging at scale.*

title: Hugging Face’s New AI Biology Model Lets You Chat With DNA
excerpt: The new open-source model speaks the language of DNA and can help researchers understand the effects of any changes on gene activity and health.
title_en: Hugging Face’s New AI Biology Model Lets You Chat With DNA
excerpt_en: The new open-source model speaks the language of DNA and can help researchers understand the effects of any changes on gene activity and health.
content_en:
The AI platform Hugging Face on Thursday released a new open model for understanding DNA that can run locally on a laptop.

Developed in collaboration with researchers at Zhongguancun Academy in China and the University of Naples Federico II in Italy, the model is trained on genomic sequences and natural language so that people can ask questions about the effects of DNA changes on gene activity and health and get conversational answers in return.

Lewis Tunstall, a senior research scientist at Hugging Face, says the tool is meant to help researchers design new drugs and genetic therapies, and it could potentially aid patients in interpreting their own genomes.

“We've unlocked a new capability in language models, which is fundamentally about being able to chat with DNA,” he says of the new model, dubbed Carbon-X. Using natural language means even nontechnical users “can actually ask questions about DNA that wouldn't be accessible through any other tool.”

Known as essentially GitHub for AI models, Hugging Face provides a library of readymade AI tools and a platform for running primarily open-weight and open-source AI applications for developers, researchers, businesses, and people who want to experiment with AI without building everything from scratch. In September, Nvidia agreed to acquire the company for nearly $13 billion. (Hugging Face was also at the center of a major hack by OpenAI’s models earlier this year.)

DNA is more like computer code than natural language. Instead of 0s and 1s, though, it uses As, Cs, Gs, and Ts to encode information. A human genome contains 6 billion of these letters. While the human genome has been sequenced end to end, scientists still don’t understand how most of it works.

Now, AI models are helping researchers decipher some of those mysteries. Last year, Google DeepMind released AlphaGenome, which predicts the effects of DNA sequences and genetic mutations but does so in a numeric format. It also requires more compute power. Evo 2, a model developed by the Arc Institute and Nvidia, along with academic partners, speaks the language of DNA and can generate entire genomes from scratch.

Carbon-X integrates both DNA and natural language in a conversational interface. Think of it like a ChatGPT for DNA.

The team started with an existing language model and expanded its vocabulary to read DNA in groups of six letters. They then continued training on 300 billion chunks of data, or tokens, that combined DNA sequences, English text, and examples linking DNA to biological descriptions. The DNA sequences came from mammals (including humans), other vertebrates, invertebrates, plants, fungi, and protozoa. Tunstall says the team didn’t train the model on viruses because they didn’t want it to be used for potentially dangerous applications.

Users won’t be able to upload full human genomes. The model was trained to be able to ingest DNA sequences of roughly 50,000 base pairs, so users will only be able to query small parts of the genome at a time.

One of the ways scientists could use Carbon-X is to help understand whether a genetic mutation is benign or disease-causing, a key step in developing a targeted drug or genetic therapy. If an intervention targets the wrong mutation, it could be totally ineffective or, worse, cause unintended harm.

Researchers face restrictions when it comes to uploading identifiable or sensitive patient data to frontier AI models, so Tunstall says his team intentionally designed a small model with 14 billion parameters. That will allow it to run locally on the user’s hardware, rather than rely on cloud-based models. No data is sent to Hugging Face or any other company, he says.

The developers of Carbon-X caution that they haven’t validated the model yet with actual wet lab experiments, so they can’t say how accurate its predictions are.
